ps. The attached photo was taken from Eunhye's mini-homepage, unrelated to the content of this post.

Before I knew it, it was January 9, 2008.
The first-half evaluation results came out, and before I could even make new year's resolutions, a week had already flown by.

I'm reading a book about time management through a reading correspondence course.
I do wonder a little if it's actually helping, but

the personal project I decided to start a week ago, I only bought the host account for it,
and couldn't produce a single page of a book, a single line of code, or a single page of documentation.

I decided to exercise in the morning,
but thanks to always going to bed late...
or using overtime as an excuse, I couldn't get myself up in the early morning.

It feels like it's already the end of December,
and after just one week, I'm already feeling self-reproachful.

I shouldn't be getting lazy already...

And the book's teaching to "do what's important to me first"
doesn't just make me weigh family and career,
but rather makes me unable to let go of my lingering attachment to personal creations like drawings, novels, or games.

My mother told me
that I'm most pathetic when I'm holed up at home playing games or drawing silly pictures.

Is that so... Am I pathetic...
But... what should I do... I like it...

An internal company announcement came out, looking for someone to plan new games like Wii or NDS.
On one hand, I wanted to apply, but fear got the better of me, so I couldn't.
(Of course, abandoning the current project would also be a very, very big deal.
Although I sometimes wonder if I'm really that important to this project, I consider myself somewhat important...)

The hope of wanting to try it, contrasted with the fear of 'what if I fail?'
The regret that even if I apply, my accumulated experience in mobile, web, and character recognition development probably won't be enough.
Those thoughts come first.

Is that why, even as a small escape, or for my own comfort,
I pour my passion and desires into my so-called "pathetic creations"?

When I was young, a friend told me,
"You want to make games? You? Don't make me laugh."
What is that friend, who used to look down on me because I couldn't fight and was short, doing now?
I at least had the ability to attempt development if I put my mind to it, but in the end, I couldn't readily step onto that path of my dream.
The intensity of work in the game industry sometimes scared me, and the failures of many past game development companies made me passive.
And even now, it remains a genre I still long for,
but since my game development skills aren't outstanding like my professional experience, I think it might be difficult for me to be accepted anywhere as a rookie now.

I'm thirty now, but still... I still don't know.
What my dream is.
When I was young, I wanted to be a "robot pilot," then a "scientist," and then
after deciding "I want to be a computer programmer," I actually entered this field.
I wonder if I'm truly creating something I desire and dedicating my passion to it.
It's not that I lack enthusiasm or motivation for my current work.
But it's just that this childish thought, 'Where is my dream?' has surfaced at this point.
And the fact that I'm suddenly at an age to become an inexperienced father makes me feel bewildered.

While looking through Cyworld, I realized I had these thoughts in my mid-twenties...

{{IMG:1}}
Suddenly, I looked at the sky and saw spring had arrived.
A blue I wanted to plunge into and drown in.

Only then did it suddenly occur to me that it was 2004.

Time had already passed my mid-twenties,
leaving me behind and rushing all the way here.
2004. 02. 15

Same pattern every year.... OTL.

**Things I definitely want to do in life (Couldn't do them this year either...)**
1.  Leave behind a drawing that everyone will remember
2.  Create a program (game) that can move people
3.  Use my skills for something meaningful, beyond profit
4.  Long-term volunteer work in the Third World
5.  Look at Earth from the moon and take a picture
6.  Become a respectable father

titleEn: Korean Telecom Carriers' Absurd Sabotage of Domestic Technology
contentEn:
{{IMG:1}}
			

http://shopping.naver.com/blog/go.nhn?cat_id=00110100&nv_mid=4068796271

			
			
			
				

#### [SPH-M6200](http://shopping.naver.com/blog/go.nhn?cat_id=00110100&nv_mid=4068796271)

				Brand Samsung Anycall
				External memory, MP3, 1.3MP camera, Bar type, Bluetooth, KTF, Anycall, BlackJack, Smartphone, 2.3-inch, 65k TFT LCD, QVGA, 40 polyphonic, Video call, Bluetooth, 1.3MP camera, Multitasking, MP3, Wireless LAN, Mobile disk, External memory, File viewer, Mobile printing
				**Rating** 
			
		

	
	

 
		
		
		
	
Feeling bored for the first time in a while, I decided to do some window shopping for a phone, even if I couldn't buy one.
 
Conditions:
 1) Must play videos
 2) Easy contact management
 3) Capable of long text input like documents
 4) Must have terrestrial DMB
 5) Must be a phone
 6) Option: Navigation expansion
 
Considering these conditions, it turns out only a smartphone fits ㅡㅡ;
I tried carrying a laptop to do document work, but concluded that even a 12-inch one was too much to pull out and use whenever I wanted.
So, the cheapest way to buy one is to choose a model integrated with a phone.
Therefore, I'm back to smartphones.
 
If the U160 had long text input, I probably would have chosen it...
So, as I was trying to choose a smartphone...
 
A new necessity emerged:
 7) Shouldn't it have Wifi?
After all, if it's a smartphone, my environment at home or work has wireless LAN...
 
So I looked it up ㅡㅡ;
Among recent phones that support Wi-Fi, the only one is Samsung's SCH-m620/m6200 BlackJack.
Models like Bluebird's BM500, which were barely released through group purchases thanks to netizens, couldn't even be launched.
(That's why it's not even in Naver's product database. Since it was released through group purchases, it circulates as skins or databases. Used ones have become rare.)
LG's recent C1 also removed Wi-Fi.
 
Apparently, Wi-Fi is considered a model that harms the profits of mobile carriers.
 
What on earth are they doing? ㅡㅡ;
Consumers want it, the technology exists, and if it spreads, the wireless internet market would obviously explode...
It just feels like they're blocking it.
In fact, integrating Wi-Fi isn't difficult not just for smartphones, but for existing mobile phones too.
 
These days, wireless internet APs are everywhere.
Naver has a wireless team, but I understand their profits are almost zero.
The same goes for other portals.
 
What could be the reason?
 
In Japan, wireless internet users have already surpassed wired internet users.
Isn't Korea's wireless infrastructure already excellent?
Even without using 3G, we can already enjoy a sufficiently limited wireless environment using APs.
The original purpose of 3G was "mobile" wireless communication.
It's not "fixed" wireless communication.
 
Yet, blocking Wi-Fi, which serves as "fixed" wireless communication, is truly absurd.
 
Korea's wireless internet speed is already the best in the world.
I acknowledge that.
 
However, it's already difficult to say that we have a high level of content and users globally.
How long must Korea's excellent technologies and competitive products disappear without even reaching the market, all to protect the narrow-minded interests of carriers fighting over their share in this small country?
 
The BlackJack probably came out because it was a global hit product for Samsung.
There are also rumors that the BlackJack 2 will remove Wi-Fi.
Some say it's due to interference from the built-in GPS...
Others say it's another conspiracy by the carriers...
 
Google's Android. Well, I'm skeptical too.
Korea might be excluded by the carriers.
 
Even when developing phones, I was annoyed by the ridiculous spec restrictions demanded by those carriers...
I quit phone development and had almost forgotten about it, but now it's making me angry again.
 
Next time I change my phone, I'll have to find a used BM500 or BlackJack ㅡㅡ;

titleEn: My Thoughts on the Recent Presidential Election Results
contentEn:
First, I write this post stating that I am a supporter of Moon Kook-hyun.
****
**1. BBK**
The biggest issue in this presidential election was BBK. However, I don't think BBK was a bad hand for Lee Myung-bak.
The Grand United Democratic New Party was busy promoting Lee Myung-bak's face rather than Chung Dong-young's, and all other issues were buried under BBK.
Yesterday, when I went to Gangnam for a year-end party, a vehicle supporting Chung Dong-young was loudly promoting Lee Myung-bak the entire time it passed by.
My friends even joked, "Is that a vehicle supporting Lee Myung-bak?"
With the votes for Lee Myung-bak that would drop due to BBK already having fallen away, there was nothing more to uncover, in fact.
Therefore, those who would be disappointed by Lee Myung-bak had already turned away long ago, and with the special prosecutor, Kim Kyung-jun,
it was unreasonable from the start to expect the public to make any extraordinary judgment in a situation where neither the media, the prosecution, the New Party, the Grand National Party, nor Lee Myung-bak himself could be trusted,
and the root cause, in fact, lay with the New Party.

It was, in fact, the New Party and the pro-government bloc that ruined the policy election,

While it was good that candidate Moon also appeared on TV to attack BBK, in a situation where his name recognition was already low, bringing up BBK
could not create differentiation, and its effect, as mentioned before, was bound to be weak.

Therefore, BBK ultimately became an opportunity for candidate Lee Myung-bak to suppress other issues or policy weaknesses.
There will continue to be noise about BBK, but will even the New Party persistently cling to it now that the presidential election is over?

Furthermore, personally, I believe it is right to unite our strength now that a new government has been inaugurated.
At the very least, the public will bear all the damage from that confusion.

**2. Media**
My regret regarding the media is what I felt most strongly as a supporter of candidate Moon.
Candidate Lee dominated most of the media. This was a power driven by immense financial resources and party strength,
and above all, in a situation where he monopolized major newspapers like Chosun, Joongang, and Dong-a, as well as TV broadcasts,
it was difficult to harbor animosity towards candidate Lee unless one meticulously examined the internet, OhmyNews, or Hankyoreh.
There were some in-depth TV special programs, but as seen from the 60% voter turnout, the interest in the presidential election itself probably didn't attract much attention.

Furthermore, the power of the internet was completely blocked from the start, with no time for it to coalesce due to election laws,
leading to a significant reduction in new attempts such as UCC (User Created Content) and blogger activities representing participation and sharing, which are characteristic of Web 2.0, thus preventing a new experiment in internet democracy from being carried out.
As someone working in internet-related fields, I feel regret about this.

After the election, hearing a certain candidate claim to have gained support from the internet made me chuckle a bit.
And if the New Party had quickly recognized this trend on the internet, they would have probably anticipated their defeat.

As discussed in a certain TV program, I felt that media outlets supporting a specific candidate should rather openly declare their support for that candidate.
Furthermore, as someone who was closely observing candidate Moon's actions, I clearly saw how much his intentions were distorted by the media, which only represented the positions of the New Party or the Grand National Party.

**3. A Warning to Existing Political Forces**
The 40% abstention rate, Heo Kyung-young's 0.4% of the vote... Moon Kook-hyun's 5.8% – these represent disappointment and a warning to existing political forces.
While some might hope to 'sandwich' Moon Kook-hyun as a pro-government candidate, a significant portion of Moon's supporters are those who dislike both the New Party and the Grand National Party.
The reason candidate Moon refused unification was because he understood his support base well,
and while candidate Chung was not unaware of that fact, he likely knew that votes eroding candidate Lee dues to BBK would not ultimately coalesce around candidate Chung.
Furthermore, by continuing to support the Creative Korea Party even after the defeat, Moon's supporters clearly demonstrate their hope for the emergence of a new force.

This means that existing political forces, regardless of whether they won or lost, should recognize that the Creative Korea Party's distinctiveness serves as a good indicator of what they themselves lack.
Heo Kyung-young's 0.4% is also the result of the 'netizen sentiment' of those who feel extreme disillusionment with politics and would rather cast their vote for someone who brings laughter.

Conversely, Lee In-je's 0.7% and Kwon Young-gil's 3% represent the public's disappointment with the old system.

**4. The Future**
I hope that the incoming government of candidate Lee Myung-bak will be well aware of the public's warnings mentioned above and govern accordingly.
I hope they truly uphold the public's aversion to corruption, address the issues of small and medium-sized enterprises, and adhere to the "pragmatism" they advocated.

I also hope that the other defeated parties will unite their strength for the nation.
I clearly saw how, when the Grand National Party strongly opposed and turned against the Roh administration, even sound policies faltered and struggled.
In fact, it cannot be denied that a significant portion of the Roh administration's policy failures were the responsibility of the Grand National Party. No matter how much they shouted, "Roh Moo-hyun was the president!", they were a massive opposition party,
and it is an undeniable fact that they wielded power beyond that of the president.

**5. Hopes and Expectations for Candidate Moon**
I personally hoped that candidate Moon, who funded his campaign with his own money, would exceed 15% and recover all the costs invested in the election,
but I understand that this did not materialize, leading to financial difficulties.
However, the 5.8% who supported you are still looking to you.
At the year-end party yesterday, a friend told me that the reason he didn't support candidate Moon was that he couldn't cast a vote based solely on one person.
He said he didn't know who was around candidate Moon and that there was a lack of a talent pool.
I couldn't help but agree with that statement.

If candidate Moon had become president this time, things would have been even more serious.
The birth of another Roh Moo-hyun administration. That would have been the conclusion. The Grand National Party and the New Party would have jointly rebelled against candidate Moon.
A 5.8% approval rating created from nothing is by no means small.
Candidate Moon surpassed Kwon Young-gil and Lee In-je. Although the Democratic Labor Party still has a 10% approval rating,
I hope the Creative Korea Party will soon achieve that.

titleEn: I have a view on war, but
contentEn:
[http://news.naver.com/main/read.nhn?mode=LS2D&mid=sec&sid1=106&sid2=222&oid=023&aid=0000297628](http://news.naver.com/main/read.nhn?mode=LS2D&mid=sec&sid1=106&sid2=222&oid=023&aid=0000297628)
 
 
I wonder if this professor has truly watched Japanese anime properly.
First, to understand the war perspective in anime, one must first understand a bit about the Japanese people's history and spiritual views.
One must also understand the author's tendencies.

Space Battleship Yamato, Sgt. Frog. These animations are indeed right-wing.
However, anime centered around fighting, such as Dragon Ball or school-themed works,
contain the samurai spirit, but there is no link connecting the samurai spirit to militarism.
(This is not a question of whether the samurai spirit is right or wrong, but simply that it is a different story from militarism.)
Rather, if one looks at the war perspective, fighting anime like Dragon Ball are closer to anarchism or anti-government views.

In the case of Astro Boy, like Rambo, it is inherently an anime for Japanese people to
overcome defeatism.
However, its conclusion does not lead to militarism.
Rather, if you look at his other works, militarism is defeated.

While many Japanese animations glorify militarism, it is also true that, conversely,
they depict it as an evil force.

The image of "military = evil"
rather reflects the historical context of Japanese people who lost trust in their government due to the defeat in World War II.
Something that was once believed to be right collapses.
This structure is effective in portraying multi-dimensional characters,
but it also makes viewers question whether what they believe is true.

Conversely, one might think that defeated Japan might not be evil,
but in fact, at its core, American hegemony and Japanese militarism are inevitably depicted in the same light.

Akira is also a very significant work in Japan's war history.
It's not about the World War II era, but a story between generations who didn't experience war after World War II.

What about Japan today?
As stated in Patlabor, specifically,
Japan is not at war, but it says that war has already begun,
and that the responsibility lies with the Japanese people themselves.

Conversely, Korean animations are not getting this serious.
This is due to low cultural diversity, and

the reality that animation is still perceived as children's literature.
There are no true "authors" yet in Korean animation.

If we are to talk about militarism, Korean animation cannot be free from it either.
During the Park Chung-hee era, works like Taekwon V, Dooly the Little Dinosaur, etc.,
were undeniably produced as ideological animations containing anti-communist ideas.

So what about today?
Are we producing as diverse stories as Japan?
We are still at the crawling stage.

It is too early to be proud of having promoted our culture by creating just one work like "The Legend of the Four Guardian Gods."
Compared to what Japan has achieved, we still have a long way to go.

The issue is not the quality of the work.
It's about how many Korean artists, through this Hallyu, can expand their artistic world globally.

A Korean artist is ultimately Korean.
A Japanese artist is Japanese.

Therefore, no matter what artistic consciousness they create with,
they interpret the same problems in their own way.

If so, at the very least, cultural diversity is an indispensable element of culture.

In that regard, I rather envy Japan.
To watch Japanese animation, curse it as "militaristic," and push everything into that category
is another form of defeatism.

Our criticism is just an empty echo in a time when we should be learning from their strengths and promoting our own.

Whether it's Japanese, American, Russian, or Korean,
culture should not be interpreted monolithically.

Because just as every character is multi-dimensional, so is the author.

If the professor were to publish a paper, it would have been better if he had analyzed "anti-militarism" or
"anarchist" animations with almost equal weight alongside "militarism,"

Wouldn't that have opened the eyes of Koreans even more?

I went to candidate Lee Myung-bak's blog and left some comments.
And of course, I even sent a trackback, so I went back to his blog to see if there were any replies or comments.
 
{{IMG:1}}
Mr. Lee Myung-bak says he doesn't want my post.
 
I didn't swear or raise any suspicions...
If I pointed out something incorrectly, you should at least reply...
Then why did you open a blog?
 
If someone swears or speaks disrespectfully, then delete it.
That's correct. But shouldn't you listen and respond to parts where people speak respectfully and point things out?
Or, shouldn't there be a discussion with candidate Lee's supporters, allowing it to function as public opinion,
and isn't the purpose of internet public opinion to create better conclusions?
 
The conclusion is, "I don't want to hear it."
 
If someone like this really becomes president...
Even Roh Moo-hyun sometimes ignored the public's voice, which was frustrating...

Mr. Lee Myung-bak. Don't do this, just close your blog.
Blogs are for exchanging opinions, and presidents and candidates are there to listen to the voices of the people.
